title: 7. Data mesh
summary: A socio-technical architecture in which business domains own and publish data products on a self-serve platform, under federated governance enforced as code.

blocks.text: 43.1 Context and the problem it solved

Central data teams in large organisations became bottlenecks. Dozens of domains (orders, payments, logistics, marketing) produced data, one team of a few dozen engineers ingested and modelled all of it, and the backlog grew faster than the team. The central team also lacked domain knowledge, so pipelines broke silently when a source changed meaning.

Data mesh, formulated by Zhamak Dehghani around 2019, answers with four principles: **domain ownership** of analytical data, **data as a product**, a **self-serve data platform**, and **federated computational governance**. It is an organisational architecture first. It is not a product you buy: the technology underneath can be a lakehouse, a warehouse or both; what changes is who owns what.

blocks.title: Data mesh planes

layers.label: Consumers
layers.sub: analysts, other domains, ML teams, semantic layer

layers.label: Mesh experience plane
layers.sub: product catalog, discovery, lineage across products, access requests

layers.label: Data products
layers.sub: per domain: code, data, metadata, contract, output ports, SLOs

layers.label: Product developer plane
layers.sub: templates to build, test, deploy and version a product

layers.label: Infrastructure plane
layers.sub: storage, Iceberg catalog, Snowflake accounts, compute, IAM, CI/CD

blocks.caption: The platform team owns the bottom planes; domain teams own the products; governance spans all.

blocks.text: A **data product** is the architectural quantum: the data, the code that produces it, its metadata and its contract, deployed together. It consumes through **input ports** and exposes **output ports**: the stable interfaces consumers read. A product can have several output ports for the same data, for example an Iceberg table for Spark users and a Snowflake share for analysts. Internal tables behind the ports are private and may change freely.

Products are classed roughly as **source-aligned** (orders as the orders domain sees them), **aggregate** (a customer 360 combining several domains) and **consumer-aligned** (a churn feature set built for one use). Aggregate products need a clear owner; they are where meshes quietly re-centralise.

blocks.text: 43.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

The medallion layers do not disappear; they move inside each product. A domain's bronze and silver are private implementation; its output port usually corresponds to a gold-quality table or a conformed silver entity. There is no global silver layer built by one team, which is the point and also the main risk: conformed dimensions such as customer or product must be agreed across domains or every join between products becomes a negotiation.

items: **Global identifiers** (customer_id, product_sku) and their formats are governance decisions, not domain decisions.
**Polysemes** (a 'customer' in marketing versus billing) are modelled explicitly: each domain publishes its view, and an aggregate product owns the reconciled one.
**Versioning:** breaking changes go to a new port version (for example `orders_v2`), with the old one kept for an agreed deprecation window.
**Semantic models** sit on output ports. Domain-level metrics can live with the domain; enterprise metrics (revenue, active customers) need one owner, or every domain defines them differently.

blocks.title: Illustrative data contract for an output port (generic format)
blocks.text:
product: orders
domain: commerce
owner: commerce-data-team
output_ports:
  - name: orders_v1
    type: iceberg_table
    location: catalog.commerce.orders_v1
  - name: orders_v1_share
    type: snowflake_share
schema:
  - {name: order_id, type: string, required: true, unique: true}
  - {name: customer_id, type: string, required: true}
  - {name: order_total, type: decimal(18,2), description: gross amount incl. VAT}
  - {name: ordered_at, type: timestamp}
slo:
  freshness: 1h
  completeness_check: daily row count within 5% of source
classification: contains customer_id (pseudonymous)
deprecation_policy: 90 days notice for breaking changes

Contract formats are still converging (the Open Data Contract Standard and the Data Contract Specification are two examples). Choose one and generate checks from it in CI rather than maintaining contracts as documentation that drifts. See chapter 33.

Each domain ingests its own sources, usually with platform-provided templates for CDC and batch loading. Orchestration is per product, but cross-product dependencies exist, so the platform needs event- or asset-based triggering (a product rebuilds when an upstream product publishes a new version) rather than one global DAG. Dagster assets, Airflow datasets or catalog events can serve this.

Serving is where **Iceberg** and **Snowflake** fit naturally. An Iceberg table registered in a shared REST catalog is an engine-neutral output port: any domain can read it from Spark, Trino or Snowflake without a copy. Snowflake secure data sharing and listings provide zero-copy output ports between Snowflake accounts, with the producer controlling access. Many meshes use both: Iceberg for engine neutrality, shares for Snowflake-native consumers.

blocks.text: A frequent failure is the 'mesh by renaming': the central team's tables are relabelled as data products and assigned to domains on paper, with no change in staffing or accountability. Nothing improves, and the catalog fills with products nobody maintains.
43.7 When to choose it, and when not

items: Choose it when there are many domains (roughly ten or more) with distinct data and the central team is the proven bottleneck.
Choose it when domains have, or can fund, engineers who will own data products as part of their job.
Choose it when leadership will back a funded platform team and enforce governance standards.
Avoid it in small or medium organisations where one central team keeps up; a well-run lakehouse or warehouse is cheaper.
Avoid it when data literacy in domains is low, or when the real problem is poor tooling rather than organisational scale.
Consider a partial mesh: domain ownership of source-aligned products, central ownership of enterprise metrics.

blocks.title: Marketplace with twelve domains
blocks.text: A marketplace had a 20-person central data team and a six-month backlog. It created a platform team that offered a product template (dbt project, Iceberg output port, contract file, CI checks) and moved source-aligned products to the domains owning the sources. Enterprise metrics stayed with a central analytics team that consumed output ports.
items: Lead time for new data fell from months to weeks where domains had engineers
Two domains without engineers stayed centrally served
Customer_id format was standardised before migration

blocks.title: Decide what to decentralise
blocks.text: An insurer has five domains (policies, claims, billing, customer, marketing) and an eight-person central data team that is keeping up but slowly. Leadership wants a data mesh. Decide which, if any, products should move to domains, what the platform must provide first, which governance rules must be computational from day one and what signals would tell you after a year that the change failed.
hints: Count which domains have engineering capacity
Think about which identifiers and classifications must be global
Consider whether the problem is scale or something else

items: Data mesh is organisational: domain ownership, data as a product, self-serve platform, federated computational governance.
A data product bundles data, code, metadata and a contract, exposed through versioned output ports.
Iceberg tables in a shared catalog and Snowflake shares are natural output ports.
Global identifiers and enterprise metrics still need central decisions.
Without domain capacity and a strong platform, a mesh degrades into unowned silos.

blocks.q: What is an output port of a data product?
options: The orchestrator job that builds the product
The private silver table used internally
The source system the product reads from
A stable, contracted interface through which consumers read the product's data
blocks.explain: Output ports are the published, versioned interfaces. Sources feed input ports, and internal tables are deliberately private so they can change without breaking consumers.

blocks.q: Which of these is the strongest signal that a company is not ready for a data mesh?
options: It uses both Snowflake and Iceberg
It already has a data catalog
Most domains have no engineers and see data products as extra work
It has more than ten business domains
blocks.explain: Domain ownership requires capacity and accountability in the domains. Many domains and mixed technology are typical of mesh adopters, not blockers.

blocks.q: What does 'computational' mean in federated computational governance?
options: Each domain writes its own security policies independently
Policies are automated and enforced by the platform, for example as CI checks and tag-based masking
Governance decisions are made by a committee of data scientists
blocks.explain: Global rules are agreed federally and then encoded so the platform enforces them automatically. Independent per-domain policies is the failure mode, not the principle.

blocks.q: The orders domain must rename a column in its output port. What is the mesh-appropriate approach?
options: Publish a new port version and keep the old one for the agreed deprecation window
Ask consumers to read the internal silver table instead
Let the central team patch all downstream queries
Rename it in place and notify consumers afterwards
blocks.explain: Versioned ports with deprecation windows let domains change without breaking consumers. In-place renames cascade failures, and exposing internals defeats the port abstraction.
